title: One Body, Many Churches
subtitle: A Theology of Unity for a Fractured Church
blurb: The church Jesus prayed for is one. The church the world sees is splintered into thousands of pieces, each certain it holds the center. This book holds two truths the modern church keeps tearing apart: that the body of Christ is genuinely one, and that the differences between churches are genuinely real — and it refuses the two cheap exits of sectarian pride and mushy relativism.

chapters.title: The Prayer He Prayed Last
chapters.summary: On the night before His death, Jesus prayed not for the church's success or survival but for its unity. We have spent two thousand years arranging that prayer at the bottom of our priorities.
chapters.body:
There is a difference between what a man says when he has time and what a man says when he is almost out of it. The deathbed clarifies. The last hours strip a life down to the few things that were always load-bearing, and everything else falls away as the freight it always was.

On the night before the crucifixion, in the seventeenth chapter of John, Jesus prays. He has washed the feet. He has handed over the bread and the cup. He has told them He is going where they cannot follow. And then, with the garden waiting and the soldiers coming, He turns from the disciples to the Father and prays not for Himself, and not only for the eleven in the room, but for everyone who would ever believe through their word. For us. He prays for us by name without using our names.

And what does He ask for? Not their comfort. Not their numerical growth. Not their doctrinal precision, though He cares about truth more than we do. He asks for their oneness. "That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us" (John 17:21). He grounds the request in the deepest reality there is — the unity of the Father and the Son — and He asks that the church reflect it.

Then He says the part we have learned to read past. "So that the world may believe that you have sent me" (John 17:21). The unity is not decorative. It is evidential. He stakes the credibility of His own mission on whether His people are one.

I came to faith out of atheism. I know what the watching world is watching for. I spent years on the outside, and I can tell you the church's divisions were never an abstraction to me. They were Exhibit A. If these people cannot agree on the God they claim transformed them, why would I believe the God is real? I did not phrase it that cleanly at the time. But the logic was already doing its work under the surface, and Jesus named that exact logic in His prayer. The world reads our unity as a verdict on our message.

We have spent twenty centuries not giving Him what He asked for.

I want to be careful here, because there is a cheap way to feel this and a costly way. The cheap way treats the prayer as a guilt trip and then changes nothing — a sigh, a wish that everyone would just get along, a vague warmth toward the church down the street whose name we cannot remember. The costly way asks what kind of unity He was actually praying for, and whether it is the kind we have any intention of pursuing.

Because notice what He does not pray for. He does not pray that they would all think identically. He does not pray that they would collapse into a single institution under a single human authority. The unity He invokes is the unity of the Father and the Son — and the Father is not the Son. They are one without being the same. The pattern of the Trinity is the pattern He hands us: distinction held inside an unbreakable oneness. Not sameness. Oneness. The difference between those two words is the difference between this book and the well-meaning mush most of us reach for instead.

Eugene Peterson spent his life insisting that the local congregation, with all its tedium and disappointment, is where the gospel actually gets lived. He was right. But the congregation is not the whole. It is a cell in a body, and a cell that imagines itself the entire organism has a name in medicine, and the name is not flattering. The temptation of every faithful local church is to mistake its own walls for the borders of the kingdom.

Consider how strange our situation would look to the apostle who wrote John 17 down. The believers of the first three centuries understood themselves to be one church scattered across the empire, persecuted as one, confessing one Lord, breaking one bread. When Cyprian wrote in the third century that there is no salvation outside the church, he was not making a denominational claim. There were no denominations. There was the church. To leave it was to leave Christ, because Christ had one body, not a marketplace of competing bodies among which a consumer might shop.

I am not romanticizing the early church. It had its factions, its heresies, its bitter councils. Paul wrote First Corinthians precisely because a congregation was already tearing itself into parties — I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Cephas (1 Corinthians 1:12). The disease is old. But the early church at least knew it was a disease. We have learned to call it freedom.

Here is where the prayer presses on me as a pastor, and not only on the church in the abstract. I lead a Baptist congregation in Michigan. I founded a network of pastors that crosses church lines. Every week I make decisions about whom to partner with, whom to platform, whom to keep at arm's length. And I have to ask myself whether those decisions are governed by the prayer of John 17 or by something smaller — by tribe, by comfort, by the quiet pleasure of being among people who already agree with me.

The honest answer is that it is often the smaller thing. We did this. I did this. The fractured church is not an inheritance handed to me by previous generations that I am merely managing; it is a project I contribute to every time I find it easier to dismiss a brother than to understand him.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote *Life Together* out of an underground seminary, in a Germany where the church had splintered along lines of cowardice and conviction. He knew that Christian community is not an ideal we construct but a reality God has already made in Christ — and that the great enemy of real community is our dream of what community should be. We come to the body of Christ with our preferences and call them principles. We mistake our taste for theology. And we walk away from one another over things the cross never authorized us to walk away from.

The prayer He prayed last is still unanswered in any way the watching world can see. That is the weight this book begins under. Not a strategy for getting churches to cooperate. A question about whether we mean to give the dying Christ the one thing He asked for, or whether we will keep arranging it at the bottom of the list, beneath our buildings and our brands and our certainty that we, of all the splinters, are the one He really had in mind.

He had all of them in mind. That is the scandal. That is the hope.
chapters.verdict: He asked for one thing on His last night, and we have spent twenty centuries not giving it to Him.
reflect: What do you actually believe Jesus was asking for in John 17:21 — and have you ever ordered your life around it?
When you picture "the church," do you picture your congregation, your denomination, or something larger than both?
What would change in how you speak about other Christians if you believed their unity with you was something Jesus prayed for?

chapters.title: One Lord, One Faith, One Baptism
chapters.summary: Before unity is a project to achieve, it is a fact to confess. Ephesians 4 names seven things that are already one — and our calling is to live up to a oneness that already exists.
chapters.body:
Paul does not begin the fourth chapter of Ephesians with a program. He begins with a prisoner. "I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called" (Ephesians 4:1). The man writing about unity is in chains, and he writes about it with a gentleness that has clearly cost him something. He names the virtues that hold a fractured people together — humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another in love (Ephesians 4:2). These are not the virtues of people who agree about everything. They are the virtues required precisely because we do not.

Then he gives the foundation, and it is the most important paragraph in any theology of the church. "There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all" (Ephesians 4:4–6).

Seven ones. Count them. Body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God and Father. Paul does not say there should be one body. He says there is one body. The unity is not in the future tense. It is in the indicative. It is a fact about reality, as fixed as the resurrection, as settled as the throne.

This changes everything about how we approach the problem. We are not architects commissioned to build a unity that does not yet exist. We are witnesses called to stop lying about a unity that already does. The body of Christ is one whether the Baptists and the Presbyterians admit it or not. The question is not whether we will create oneness. The question is whether our lives will tell the truth about it or keep telling a more convenient lie.

Not a project. A confession.

I find this enormously freeing, and I find it terrifying, and I think both responses are correct. It is freeing because it takes the impossible weight off my shoulders. I do not have to reunite Christendom. I could not if I tried. Christ has already made His body one in Himself, and my job is the smaller, harder job of living as though that were true. It is terrifying because it removes my excuses. I cannot say the divisions are simply how things are. They are not how things are at the level that finally matters. They are how I have chosen to act in defiance of how things are.

Consider the word "baptism" in that list. Of all things to call one. The waters of baptism have divided the church as bitterly as anything — infant or believer, immersion or sprinkling, what it does and what it merely signifies. I hold convictions about this. I lead a Baptist church; my convictions are not secret. And yet Paul, knowing the church would fight about the mode and the meaning for two thousand years, writes the word *one* over all of it. Not because the differences do not exist, but because beneath the differences there is a single reality: a people marked out as belonging to the triune God, washed into the death and resurrection of one Lord.

Tim Keller often pointed to the architecture of Paul's letters — the long indicative foundation before the imperative walls go up. You see it here with perfect clarity. The "walk worthy" of verse one is built on the "there is one body" of verse four. Paul never gives a command without first laying the ground it stands on. The command to maintain unity rests entirely on the prior fact that unity exists. Take away the fact and the command becomes moralism — try harder, be nicer, get along. Keep the fact and the command becomes something else entirely: live up to what you already are.

Notice too that Paul says "maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:3). Maintain. Not achieve. Not invent. The Spirit has already made it; we are charged to keep it, to guard it, to bear with one another in a love that refuses to let it fracture on our watch. The Greek word carries the sense of guarding something precious that is under threat. The unity is real, and it is also fragile in our hands, and we are its custodians, not its creators.

Here is the line that has reorganized my thinking. The fracturing of the church is not the failure to build something. It is the failure to confess something. Every time a congregation splits over the carpet color or the worship style or the personality of the pastor, it is not failing to create a unity it never had. It is publicly denying a unity it was given. It is bearing false witness against the body of Christ.

That is a heavier charge than the one we usually level. We tend to treat division as a sad inevitability, the ecclesiastical equivalent of bad weather. Paul treats it as a contradiction of the gospel. When the Corinthians divided into parties, he did not say they had merely failed to be friendly. He asked, "Is Christ divided?" (1 Corinthians 1:13). The question is rhetorical and the answer is no — and therefore a divided church is preaching a divided Christ, which is no Christ at all.

I have to sit under this as much as anyone. The Pastors Connection Network exists because I came to believe, slowly and against my own instincts, that the pastor across town in the church I theologically disagree with is not my competitor. He confesses one Lord, one faith, one baptism. He drinks the one Spirit. If the seven ones of Ephesians 4 are true, then my relationship to him is not optional warmth I might extend if I am feeling generous. It is the truth I am obligated to confess with my conduct.

The reformer Richard Baxter is often credited with the formula: in essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity. We will spend later chapters trying to work out which things are which, because that is precisely where the formula stops being easy. But the formula has a floor under it, and Ephesians 4 is the floor. There is one body. That is not negotiable. That is not one of the things on which liberty operates. It is the bedrock the whole structure stands on.

We are not asked to manufacture the church's unity. We are asked to stop contradicting it. The body is one. The only question left is whether your life and mine will tell the truth.
chapters.verdict: We are not asked to manufacture the church's unity; we are asked to stop contradicting it.
reflect: Which of the seven "ones" in Ephesians 4:4–6 do you most easily forget when you think about Christians who differ from you?
Is the unity you long for something you think the church must build, or something you believe God has already made?
Where have you treated a matter of preference as if it were a matter of the one faith?

chapters.title: The Body and Its Parts
chapters.summary: First Corinthians 12 does not describe a uniform mass but a body of radically different members, and it insists that the difference is the design, not the defect.
chapters.body:
The image Paul reaches for when he wants to describe the church is not an army, where uniformity is the point. It is not a building, though he uses that elsewhere. When the unity of the church is most under threat, in the most divided congregation he wrote to, Paul reaches for the body. "For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ" (1 Corinthians 12:12).

Read that sentence slowly, because it is doing something our instincts resist. It does not say the body overcomes its many parts to achieve unity. It says the many parts *are* the one body. The plurality is not the problem to be solved. The plurality is the form the unity takes. A body with one kind of part is not a more unified body. It is a tumor.

Paul presses the image until it becomes almost comic. "If the foot should say, 'Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,' that would not make it any less a part of the body" (1 Corinthians 12:15). The foot's sense of inferiority does not unmake its membership. And then the other direction: "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you'" (1 Corinthians 12:21). The eye's sense of superiority does not unmake the hand's necessity. Paul attacks the two diseases of the divided church from both ends — the false humility that withdraws and the false pride that dismisses.

Both of those are with us. The small church that decides it does not really count, that the work happens elsewhere, in the big ministries with the platforms — that is the foot saying it is not a hand. And the prominent church or tradition that looks down the road at the other kind of Christian and concludes there is nothing to learn there, no gift worth receiving, no need to be met — that is the eye telling the hand it is dispensable. I have been both. I have felt my small Michigan congregation was too obscure to matter, and I have felt, in uglier moments, that I had nothing to receive from believers whose theology I had already decided was beneath mine. Both are the same sin wearing different clothes. Both deny the body.

A church that wants every member to be identical does not want a body. It wants a corpse.

What strikes me hardest in this chapter is the role Paul assigns to God. "But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:18). The arranging is God's work, and God's choice. The diversity of the body is not an accident of fallen history that we are slowly correcting toward sameness. It is the deliberate composition of the one who knows what a body needs. When I look at the strange variety of the global church — the contemplative monastery and the storefront Pentecostal congregation, the high liturgy and the bare meeting room, the African Anglican and the Korean Presbyterian and the Appalachian Baptist — I am looking at an arrangement God chose.

That does not mean every difference is good. Some divisions are sin, and we will be honest about that throughout this book. Paul is not blessing the parties of Corinth. But there is a difference between division and diversity, and we constantly confuse the two. Division is the body tearing itself apart. Diversity is the body being what a body is. The contemplative tradition has kept alive a depth of prayer my own tradition often neglects. The liturgical traditions have guarded the church's memory across centuries when revivalism forgot it. The Pentecostal movement recovered an expectancy about the Spirit that the rationalist wings of Protestantism had quietly abandoned. The eye genuinely needs the hand. I genuinely need the parts of the body that are not like me.

Here is the part I least want to write. Paul says, "On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable" (1 Corinthians 12:22). The weaker parts. The unimpressive parts. The ones we are tempted to be embarrassed by. He says God has given greater honor to the part that lacked it, "that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). The cure for division, in Paul's mind, is honoring the part you were tempted to despise. Not tolerating it. Honoring it.

I think of the churches the broader evangelical world finds embarrassing. The tiny rural congregations with no platform and no relevance. The traditions whose practices strike us as strange. The believers whose cultural expression of faith looks nothing like ours. Paul's instruction is not to tolerate them while waiting for them to modernize. It is to grant them greater honor, precisely because they are the parts the body is tempted to disdain.

Walter Brueggemann spent his career reading the prophets, and the prophets were forever attacking the establishment's contempt for the weak. The same prophetic edge runs through First Corinthians 12. The strong members assume the body is essentially theirs and the weak ones are guests. Paul flips it. The weak are indispensable. The body cannot be the body without them. This is not sentimentality about the underdog. It is a structural claim about how the body of Christ is actually composed and what it actually needs to function.

And then the sentence that lands the whole chapter: "If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together" (1 Corinthians 12:26). The test of whether you actually believe the church is one body is whether the suffering of a church not your own registers as your suffering. When the persecuted believers in a country you will never visit are imprisoned, does it cost you anything? When a tradition you disagree with is slandered, do you defend it as your own? Or do you feel, somewhere beneath the theology you would profess, a small satisfaction that it was them and not you?

The honest answer indicts me. I have read of suffering churches and felt sympathy at the distance one feels for strangers, not the agony one feels for one's own body. I have heard a denomination I disagree with mocked and felt the quiet pull of the joke before I felt the loyalty of a fellow member. The doctrine of the one body is not hard to affirm. It is hard to feel. And until it is felt — until another church's wound aches in my own flesh — I have not really believed it. I have only recited it.

The body is one. The parts are many. And the many are not the obstacle to the one. They are the only form the one was ever going to take.
chapters.verdict: A church that wants every member to be identical does not want a body; it wants a corpse.
reflect: When you encounter a Christian tradition very different from yours, is your first instinct to see a rival or a member of the same body?
What gift or strength does another church possess that yours genuinely lacks?
Have you ever said, in effect, "I have no need of you" to another part of Christ's body?

chapters.title: Unity Is Not Uniformity
chapters.summary: The deepest confusion in the church's thinking about unity is the assumption that to be one we must be the same. The Trinity teaches us otherwise.
chapters.body:
The error is so common that we have almost stopped noticing it is an error. We use the word "unity" and we mean "agreement." We say a church is unified when everyone thinks the same, votes the same, prefers the same songs and the same sermons and the same shade of carpet. And so we conclude that unity with other Christians would require us all to converge on a single set of opinions — and since that will never happen, we quietly give up on unity altogether and call our resignation realism.

But that is not the unity Scripture describes, and it is not the unity God Himself possesses.

God is one. The Shema stands at the center of Israel's faith: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). And God is three. Father, Son, and Spirit, not three masks of one actor and not three gods in a committee, but one God in three persons, distinct without division, united without collapse. The Father is not the Son. The Son is not the Spirit. And yet there are not three Gods. There is one.

This is not a riddle the church invented to torment seminary students. It is the deepest thing that can be said about reality, because it is the truest thing that can be said about God, and it is the pattern Jesus invokes when He prays for our unity. "That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you" (John 17:21). The unity of the church is meant to image the unity of the Trinity. And the unity of the Trinity is not uniformity. It is the perfect communion of genuinely distinct persons.

A God who is three and one made a church that is many and one. We keep trying to improve on Him.

The councils of the early church fought for centuries to get this language right, and they fought because they knew the stakes. At Nicaea in 325, the church confessed the Son to be of one substance with the Father — *homoousios* — against those who would make Him a lesser, created thing. The fight was not pedantry. If the Son were merely similar to the Father, the unity of God would be cheap, a partnership rather than a communion. The church insisted on the harder truth: full distinction, full unity, at once. The Nicene Creed, which most of the splintered church still confesses together, is itself a monument to the kind of unity this chapter is about — a document Baptists and Catholics and the Orthodox can stand and recite in one voice, across every later division, because it names the things that are actually one.

Now apply the pattern. If the unity of the church images the unity of God, then the unity of the church cannot mean the erasure of difference. It must mean the communion of differences. The Presbyterian and the Baptist do not become one by one of them ceasing to be what he is. They are one in Christ while remaining distinct in conviction — not despite the distinction but in a unity large enough to contain it. Uniformity would actually be a *worse* image of God, because the God we image is not undifferentiated. He is communion.

Kevin Vanhoozer has written about the church as a kind of company performing the one drama of redemption, each tradition a different production of the same play — faithful to the same script, staged in the idiom of a different people and place. I find the picture clarifying. There is one play. There is genuinely one. Wander into a performance that has rewritten the ending so that Christ does not rise, and you have not encountered a legitimate variation; you have encountered a different play, and the unity does not extend to it. But within fidelity to the script, the church has always staged the drama in many tongues and many forms, and the variety is not infidelity. It is the gospel proving it can be at home in every culture without being captured by any.

This is where I have to confess my own tradition's particular temptation. The wing of the church I come from, the free-church evangelical world, has often treated its own cultural form as though it were the gospel itself. The casual dress, the contemporary band, the conversational sermon, the suspicion of liturgy and creed and the church calendar — these are choices, and often good ones, but we have a habit of mistaking our preferences for principles and then judging the rest of the body for failing to share them. We look at a tradition that kneels and chants and follows a fixed order of worship and we conclude it must be dead, formal, going through the motions. We have made our taste into a doctrine. And in doing so we have pursued uniformity and called it unity.

The opposite error is just as real, and I do not want to dodge it. There is a kind of high-church confidence that looks at the storefront congregation with its drum kit and its raised hands and concludes that real Christianity requires the apparatus of history and sacrament, that these enthusiasts are playing at a faith they do not understand. That is the same sin from the other side. Both are demanding uniformity. Both are saying: be like me, or you are not really in.

Bonhoeffer warned against the dream of community — the ideal we carry in our heads of what the church should be, which we then impose on the real church in front of us, and which we love more than we love the actual brothers and sisters God has given us. The dream of uniformity is exactly that. It is a love for the church as we wish it were, and that love, Bonhoeffer said, is a destroyer of community, because it will tolerate no one who fails to fit the dream. The man who loves his dream of Christian community will destroy real community. The man who loves the brothers and sisters in front of him, with all their wrong opinions and irritating habits, will build it.

So what does it mean to be one with someone I will never fully agree with? It means I stop requiring agreement as the price of communion. It means I locate our unity where God actually placed it — in the one Lord, the one faith, the one baptism, the one body — and not in the secondary opinions where I keep relocating it because the secondary opinions are where I feel strong. It means I learn to say, with the whole catholic church across twenty centuries, the creed that names what is genuinely one, and then to hold my distinctives as distinctives rather than as the boundary line of the kingdom.

The hardest sentence to write is this one. Every time I have demanded that another Christian become like me before I would call him a brother, I was not defending the truth. I was defending myself. I was making my own form the measure of the gospel. And a God who is three and one stood by, having shown us a better way, while I insisted on the worse one.
chapters.verdict: A God who is three and one made a church that is many and one; we keep trying to improve on Him.
reflect: Where in your church life have you pursued sameness and called it unity?
Can you name a real difference with another Christian that you nonetheless refuse to let break fellowship?
What would it mean to be one with someone you will never fully agree with?

chapters.title: The Universal and the Local
chapters.summary: The New Testament uses one word, ekklesia, for both the church on the corner and the church across all time and space. Holding both at once is the discipline this chapter asks of us.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in Matthew where Jesus speaks of building "my church" (Matthew 16:18), singular, universal, the whole company of the redeemed across all ages, against which the gates of hell will not prevail. And there is a sentence two chapters later where He speaks of taking a matter "to the church" (Matthew 18:17), meaning the specific local assembly that can actually hear a dispute and act on it. Same word. Two referents. And the entire health of our ecclesiology depends on holding them together.

The word is *ekklesia*. It means, at root, an assembly — a gathered people, called out. And the New Testament uses it with a striking double vision. Paul writes "to the church of God that is in Corinth" (1 Corinthians 1:2), a particular body with a particular address and particular problems. And Paul writes that Christ is "head over all things to the church, which is his body" (Ephesians 1:22–23), the universal fullness of the redeemed. The local congregation is the church. The whole company of the saved is the church. Both are true, and the truth lives in the tension between them.

Lose the universal and you get a congregation that imagines itself the entire kingdom — the foot insisting it is the body, the local fellowship that cannot conceive of God working anywhere but inside its own walls and its own way of doing things. Lose the local and you get a Christianity of the clouds, a "universal church" that exists only as an idea, a way of belonging to everyone in general and no one in particular, of loving the abstract church precisely so that you never have to be inconvenienced by the real one.

You must hold both or you will betray one.

I want to press hard on the second error, because it is the fashionable one and the one the disconnected and the wounded most often reach for. There are many believers now who have given up on the local church and kept "the universal church" as a consolation — who say they love Christ's body, the whole great invisible communion of believers everywhere, while belonging to no actual congregation, submitting to no actual elders, being known by no actual people who could tell them the truth about themselves. This is the church reduced to a feeling. And it is impossible to obey the New Testament from inside it.

Because the commands are local. Bear one another's burdens. Confess your sins to one another. Submit to those who watch over your souls. Do not neglect to meet together (Hebrews 10:25). The "one another" of the New Testament requires another in the room. You cannot bear the burden of an abstraction. You cannot be rebuked by an idea. The universal church becomes visible, becomes flesh, becomes obeyable, only as it touches the ground in a particular place with particular people whose faults you must endure and who must endure yours.

Eugene Peterson built his whole pastoral theology on this refusal to flee the local. He insisted that the pastor's calling is to this congregation, these people, this place, with all its smallness and disappointment, because that is where the gospel is incarnated and not merely admired. He was suspicious of the religious imagination that prefers the church in general to the church in particular, because the church in general never sins against you, never bores you, never lets you down — and never sanctifies you either. The grand abstract church costs nothing. The congregation costs everything. That is the point.

But Peterson would be the first to say the local is not enough by itself. The congregation that forgets it is a member of something vastly larger becomes ingrown, provincial, finally idolatrous — worshiping its own way of being the church as though no other way were legitimate. I have watched it happen. A congregation falls so in love with its own culture, its own history, its own founding pastor and founding vision, that it can no longer recognize the family resemblance in the believers across town. It says, in effect, that the church is here, and what is out there is something lesser. That is the local swallowing the universal, and it is its own kind of betrayal.

The old distinction between the visible and the invisible church helps here, if we use it carefully. The invisible church is the whole company known to God alone — every true believer across every age, the elect, the body in its final fullness. The visible church is that body as it appears in history, in actual congregations, with actual membership rolls that include both wheat and weeds. Calvin used the distinction not to let anyone off the hook but to hold two truths at once: that final membership belongs to God's knowledge, and that present obligation belongs to the visible body we can see and must join. He had no category for a Christian who belonged to the invisible church while despising the visible one. To him the visible church was our mother, and he meant it tenderly — outside her care, he said, there is no ordinary hope of growth in grace. You do not love your mother by loving the abstract idea of motherhood.

Here is the discipline the chapter asks. When I stand in my congregation on a Sunday, I am to see two things at once. I am to see these people — this widow, this restless teenager, this couple barely holding their marriage together, this family I have buried two members of. They are the church, concretely, and they have a claim on me that no abstraction could exert. And at the same time I am to see, through them and beyond them, the whole body of Christ across the earth and across the centuries, of which this small Michigan room is one living cell. The universal does not float above the local. It is present in it. This congregation is a window onto the whole.

The Pastors Connection Network grew out of exactly this double vision. A pastor who only sees his own congregation will compete with the church down the road. A pastor who only sees the universal church will love no one in particular. But a pastor who sees his congregation as a member of the one body will recognize the pastor across town as a fellow cell in the same organism — not a competitor, not a stranger, but a brother whose flourishing is his own flourishing, because they suffer and rejoice together as members of one body.

I have to repent of both errors in myself. I have loved my congregation so possessively that I forgot it was not the whole. And I have, in tired seasons, retreated into a vague affection for the "real" church somewhere out there, the spiritual one, the one that does not require me to sit through another difficult meeting with people I find exhausting. Both retreats are flights from the cross. The cross holds the local and the universal together in one body, broken for the whole and given to each particular person by name.

Hold both. Or you will betray one. And the one you betray will be the one Christ died for.
chapters.verdict: Your local church is not the whole church, and the whole church cannot be loved in the abstract; you must hold both or you will betray one.
reflect: Do you tend to over-identify with your local church or to float above all churches in a vague universalism?
How does belonging to the universal church change how you treat the local one?
What concrete commitment ties you to a particular congregation, with its particular faults?

chapters.title: Primary, Secondary, and the Wisdom to Tell Them Apart
chapters.summary: Not every doctrine carries the same weight, and the maturity of a church is largely the ability to tell a hill worth dying on from a hill we have merely grown fond of.
chapters.body:
Richard Baxter, the Puritan pastor of Kidderminster, is remembered for a sentence he may not have coined but certainly lived: in essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity. It is the most quoted formula in the theology of unity, and it is quoted so often because it is exactly right and almost useless — right because the principle is sound, useless because it tells you nothing about which things are essential.

That is the whole problem. Everyone agrees we should be united on the essentials and free on the rest. The fights are entirely about the boundary. One man's secondary issue is another man's hill to die on, and the formula by itself cannot adjudicate between them. So we have to do the harder work the formula points toward but does not perform.

Begin with the recognition that doctrines do not all carry the same weight. This is not relativism; it is plain reading. Paul tells the Corinthians that he delivered to them "as of first importance" the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3). Of first importance. The phrase assumes a second importance, a third. Paul ranks. Some things are the foundation; build wrong there and the building falls. Some things are the framing; get them wrong and the house is misshapen but standing. Some things are the paint color, and grown adults do not divide a household over paint.

A useful way to sort, though no scheme is perfect, runs in three tiers. First-order doctrines are those that define the gospel itself — the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, His bodily resurrection, justification by grace through faith, the authority of Scripture. Deny these and you have left the faith, not joined a different wing of it. These are the things the ancient creeds were written to guard, and the church spilled centuries of effort and sometimes blood to confess them rightly because everything hung on them.

Second-order doctrines are those over which true Christians genuinely divide into different churches — the mode and subjects of baptism, the form of church government, the workings of the Lord's Supper, the role of spiritual gifts, the boundaries of who may lead. These are not trivial. They are why I am a Baptist and not a Presbyterian, and the difference is real enough that we worship in different buildings on Sunday morning. But — and this is the whole point — they are not the gospel. A paedobaptist and a credobaptist disagree about something important and remain brothers in the one faith. We divide congregationally over second-order matters; we do not divide the body of Christ over them.

Third-order doctrines are the rest — eschatological timelines, worship styles, the thousand matters of prudence and preference on which Scripture either is silent or speaks softly. To divide over these is, frankly, a scandal. Paul addressed exactly this in Romans 14, where some ate meat and some did not, some kept days and some did not, and his command was not to resolve the dispute but to stop despising one another over it. "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?" (Romans 14:4). He let the disagreement stand and forbade the division.

We will answer not only for the truths we abandoned but for the trifles we divided over as though they were the truth.

Now, the obvious danger, and I will not pretend it away. Once you grant that doctrines carry different weights, you have handed every lazy and cowardly heart a tool for demoting whatever it finds inconvenient. The man who wants to keep his comfortable sin will discover that the offending doctrine is, conveniently, secondary. The church that wants to be popular will find the hard teachings drifting steadily down the tiers until nothing is left at the top but a generic kindness. This is the mush this book exists to refuse. The recognition that some doctrines are secondary must never become the assumption that no doctrine is primary.

So the question of the chapter is the question of the reflection: who decides, and how do we guard the deciding from our own preferences? Three guardrails.

First, the creeds. The church did not leave us to start from scratch. Nicaea, the great councils, the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds — these are the church's hard-won consensus on what is first-order, ratified across the very divisions we are trying to heal. When Baptists and Catholics and the Orthodox can all stand and confess the same creed, that creed marks out something genuinely essential. The creeds are not a substitute for Scripture, but they are the church's collective memory of which scriptural truths are load-bearing, and a man who decides the essentials alone, against twenty centuries of confession, should suspect himself first.

Second, the gospel test. Does denying this doctrine destroy the gospel, or merely disagree about how to live it out? If a man denies the resurrection, there is no gospel left; the matter is first-order. If a man baptizes infants, the gospel he preaches may be entirely intact even though I think his practice mistaken; the matter is second-order. The test is not "do I feel strongly about this" — we feel strongly about all sorts of things — but "does the gospel survive the disagreement."

Third, and this is the one we evade, self-suspicion. The doctrines we are most tempted to elevate to essential status are usually the ones that flatter our tribe, the ones that distinguish us from the Christians we want to feel superior to. The Pharisees were experts in this. They built fences around the law and then defended the fences as fiercely as the law, until the fence had become the thing and the law had been lost. Every tradition has its fences mistaken for foundations. The Reformed have ours. I have mine. The mature believer learns to ask, when a doctrine feels essential, whether it feels essential because the gospel hangs on it or because his identity does.

I came to faith as an adult, out of atheism, and I am grateful for one accident of that history: I had no tribal Christianity to inherit, no denominational loyalty I absorbed before I could examine it. I had to assemble my convictions from Scripture rather than from a family pew. That does not make me wiser — converts have their own blindnesses — but it left me with a permanent suspicion of the doctrine that is held mainly because it is ours. The doctrines worth dying for are not ours. They are the church's, across every age, and they do not need my tribe to defend them.

Tell the difference. The whole maturity of a church is hidden in that sentence. A church that cannot tell a foundation from a fence will either compromise the foundation, defending nothing because it has learned everything is negotiable, or defend the fences to the death, dividing the body of Christ over the color of the paint and calling it faithfulness. Both are failures of discernment. Both will be answered for.

The hill matters. Choose it well, because you will die on something, and you do not want to give your life for a fence.
chapters.verdict: We will answer not only for the truths we abandoned but for the trifles we divided over as though they were the truth.
reflect: Can you name three doctrines you would die for and three you would not divide over?
Where have you treated a secondary matter as if it were primary — and why did it feel primary to you?
Who decides what is essential, and how do you guard that judgment from your own preferences?

chapters.title: The Scandal of Division
chapters.summary: A watching world reads the church's fractures as evidence against the gospel, exactly as Jesus warned it would. The scandal is not that we disagree but that we have made disagreement our witness.
chapters.body:
I will tell you what the gospel sounded like from the outside, because I was outside, and I remember.

It sounded like a quarrel. It sounded like people who claimed to be remade by an infinite love and who could not sit at the same table. It sounded like denominations dividing and subdividing, each new fragment certain it had finally gotten right what all the others had gotten wrong, each one a fresh proof that whatever the Christians had, it did not produce the unity they kept preaching about. I did not need a clever argument against Christianity. The Christians supplied it. They could not agree on the God who had supposedly transformed them, and that fact did more to keep me an atheist than any book by any skeptic ever did.

Jesus told us this would happen. He staked it. "That they may all be one... so that the world may believe that you have sent me" (John 17:21). The logic runs in both directions. If our unity is evidence the Father sent the Son, then our division is evidence against it. He did not say it might be read that way. He built His prayer on the assumption that the world is watching the church's oneness and drawing conclusions about the gospel from it.

We have given the world its best argument against Christ. And we gave it from inside the church.

Let me be careful, because there is a false guilt available here that I do not want to peddle, and there is a true one I do not want you to escape. The false guilt says all division is sin, that any disagreement betrays the prayer, that faithfulness requires us to paper over real differences for the sake of appearances. That is not what I am saying and it is not what Scripture teaches. Paul divided from those who preached another gospel and called down a curse on them (Galatians 1:8–9). There are divisions the truth requires. To refuse them is not unity; it is cowardice wearing unity's clothes.

The true guilt is different and harder. It is that the overwhelming majority of our divisions are not the kind Galatians authorizes. They are not divisions over the gospel. They are divisions over personality, over power, over preference, over the secondary and third-order matters of the last chapter, dressed up in the language of conviction so that we can feel principled while we tear the body apart. The world cannot tell the difference between a division over the resurrection and a division over the worship band, because from the outside they look identical: Christians who cannot stay together. And most of our divisions, if we are honest, are the worship-band kind.

Consider the great fractures of history with sober eyes. The schism of 1054, when the church of the East and the church of the West finally severed communion — over genuine theological questions, yes, the procession of the Spirit, the authority of Rome, but also over politics, language, mutual contempt, and a thousand accumulated grievances that had nothing to do with the gospel and everything to do with the failure of love. The Reformation of 1517, which I believe recovered truths the medieval church had buried and which I would not undo — and which also fractured into a hundred warring factions within a generation, Protestants persecuting Protestants, the recovered gospel immediately weaponized against fellow believers. I am a son of the Reformation. I will not romanticize what it also unleashed. The recovery of justification by faith did not come with a recovery of love for the brother who read the sacraments differently, and the wars of religion that followed taught Europe to despise the faith that fueled them.

I am not competent to relitigate 1054 or 1517, and that is not the point. The point is that the church has a long habit of dividing over real things and false things alike, and of presenting all of it to the world as the natural fruit of conviction, while the world quietly concludes that conviction is the problem and walks away from Christ altogether.

Lesslie Newbigin saw this with unusual clarity. He spent decades as a missionary in India and returned to a secular West he hardly recognized, and he argued that the congregation is the hermeneutic of the gospel — the lens through which the world reads the message. The gospel is not finally believed because of arguments; it is believed because a community lives it visibly enough that the message becomes credible. And the corollary is brutal. A divided community is an unbelievable gospel. The world does not read our doctrinal statements. It reads our relationships. When those relationships are marked by faction and contempt, the doctrine becomes incredible no matter how true it is, because the people who hold it have demonstrably not been changed by it.

This is the missionary catastrophe of division, and it falls hardest exactly where the work is hardest — among the skeptics, the audience Jesus aimed His prayer at, the audience I belonged to. The Christian who is wounded but still believing can survive the spectacle of a church split; he has resources, a history with God, a reason to stay. The skeptic has no such resources. For him the split is simply data, and the data points away from Christ. Every ugly division is a sermon preached to the watching world, and the sermon is: do not believe this. These people do not believe it themselves, or it would have made them one.

I have preached that sermon. Not from the pulpit, but in the small ways that the world reads more closely than any pulpit. In the dismissive comment about another church. In the relish with which I have told a story that made a fellow pastor look foolish. In the years I let a relationship with a brother stay broken because reconciling would have cost my pride more than I wanted to pay. Someone watched. Someone always watches. And I cannot know how many were nudged a little further from Christ by the spectacle of His servants at war.

Here is the weight I want to leave you carrying. The scandal of division is not primarily that it embarrasses us. It is that it costs the very people Christ died to reach. When we fracture the body before a watching world, we are not merely failing an internal standard of niceness. We are obscuring the only evidence Jesus said would make His mission credible to outsiders. We are, in the most literal sense, hindering the salvation of the lost — not by what we teach but by how we treat one another.

The world is still watching. It read me out of the faith for years, and it read me back in, eventually, partly through Christians who refused the easy contempt, who treated their differences as family arguments and not as grounds for war. They were not perfectly united. But they were united enough that the gospel became, for me, finally believable.

What is the world learning from you?
chapters.verdict: We have given the world its best argument against Christ, and we gave it from inside the church.
reflect: What has the watching world learned about Christ from the way Christians treat one another?
Have you ever helped someone disbelieve the gospel by the way you fought another Christian?
When you defend a division, are you defending the truth or defending yourself?

chapters.title: Denominations: Gift, Sin, and Scaffolding
chapters.summary: Denominations are neither simply good nor simply evil. They are at once a sin we should mourn, a providence God has used, and a scaffold that must not be mistaken for the building.
chapters.body:
Let me say the uncomfortable thing first. Denominations are, in part, a sin. They are the institutional memory of our failures to stay together. Every separate denomination is a monument to a moment when the body of Christ could not hold, when conviction or pride or power drove a wedge that hardened into a structure. We did not get thousands of distinct Protestant bodies because the Spirit willed a thousand competing institutions. We got them because we kept dividing and then building walls around the divisions to make them permanent.

I am a Baptist. My own tradition was born partly in necessary protest and partly in the same fracturing impulse that has split it many times since. I will not pretend the existence of my denomination is a pure gift to the church. In part it is a wound the church has learned to live with, scar tissue grown over old breaks.

So we should mourn them. That is the first word, and the church rarely says it. We treat our denominational identities as though they were simply natural, simply given, as innocent as nationality. They are not innocent. They are, at least in part, the visible record of our inability to love one another well enough to stay together. Jesus prayed we would be one, and the denominational map of the church is the measure of how far His prayer remains unanswered.

That is the first word. It is not the only word.

Because God, in His mercy, does what He always does with our sin: He bends it toward good without ever calling it good. The denominations that began as failures of unity have become, in His providence, guardians of particular treasures the whole church needed kept. The Reformed traditions preserved a high view of God's sovereignty and the careful reading of the whole counsel of Scripture when others let it slide. The Anglican and Lutheran bodies kept the church's worship anchored in the historic forms and the church calendar when the free churches were happily forgetting them. The Methodists carried a passion for holiness and the poor. The Pentecostals recovered an expectancy about the Spirit's present power that the rest of us had quietly filed away as a thing that used to happen. The Anabaptists held the costly witness of peace and discipleship when establishment churches were blessing the swords of kings.

Each tradition, even in its origin as a fracture, became a steward of something. And the whole body is richer for the stewardship, even as it is poorer for the division that produced it. Both are true at once. God did not author the division. He has used it. To deny the first is to excuse our sin; to deny the second is to deny His providence. The mature church holds both without flinching.

A denomination is a tool for serving the one church. The moment it forgets that, it becomes an idol with a letterhead.

Here is the test that sorts the gift from the sin in any present moment: does the denomination exist to serve the one body of Christ, or has it begun to serve itself? Every institution drifts the same direction. It begins as a means to an end — a way to train pastors, plant churches, send missionaries, guard a doctrine, coordinate a mission across many congregations. These are good ends, and the denomination is a good scaffold for reaching them. But scaffolds have a way of forgetting they are scaffolds. The institution that was built to serve the building starts to imagine itself the building. Self-preservation replaces mission. Loyalty to the denomination replaces loyalty to Christ. The budget, the brand, the bureaucracy become things to be defended for their own sake, and the question quietly shifts from "how does this serve the kingdom" to "how does this serve us."

When that happens, the denomination has become an idol with a letterhead. It still uses the language of mission. It still prays the prayers. But its real religion is its own continuance, and it will sacrifice the unity of the wider body, and sometimes the truth itself, on the altar of institutional survival.

Augustine, writing against the Donatists in North Africa in the fourth and fifth centuries, fought a version of this. The Donatists had made their own purer communion the test of the true church, had walled themselves off as the faithful remnant against the compromised majority. Augustine insisted that the true church is a mixed body, wheat and weeds together until the harvest, and that to tear oneself away in the name of purity was itself a graver sin than the impurity one was fleeing. He loved the unity of the church more than he loved the satisfaction of being right and separate. That instinct — that unity itself is a value the schismatic always underweights — is the instinct denominationalism most needs and most lacks.

The Reformers themselves, the very men who broke with Rome, did not intend to found denominations in our sense. Calvin labored for the unity of the Protestant churches and grieved their divisions; he corresponded across Europe trying to hold the fragments together, and was bitterly disappointed when they would not cohere. The proliferation of competing bodies was not the Reformation's goal. It was its tragedy, the shadow side of its recovery. Even those who divided for the truth's sake understood division as a cost, not a triumph.

This is where my own work has had to find its footing. The Pastors Connection Network is, deliberately, not a denomination. It is a network across them — a scaffold built to serve the one body precisely by refusing to become another competing institution. I built it that way because I came to believe that what the fractured church needs is not one more flag to rally under but structures that hold the existing flags together, that treat the denominational lines as real but not ultimate, that let a Baptist and a Presbyterian and a non-denominational pastor labor side by side without anyone having to surrender his convictions or his congregation. The denominations are scaffolding. The network tries to be scaffolding that remembers it is scaffolding.

I have to examine my own loyalty, though, and so do you. The reflection question is not rhetorical: could I imagine my denomination ceasing to exist if the one church were better served without it? The honest flinch I feel at that question is itself diagnostic. If the thought of my tradition's disappearance distresses me more than the thought of the church's continued division, then I have my loves out of order. I have come to serve the scaffold rather than the building. And the scaffold, however useful, was never the thing Christ died for. He died for the church. He did not die for my denomination.

Mourn them as sin. Receive them as providence. Use them as scaffolding. But do not worship them. The day a tradition asks you to choose between its survival and the unity of Christ's body, you will discover what you actually believe the church is — and the letterhead will not save you.
chapters.verdict: A denomination is a tool for serving the one church, and the moment it forgets that, it becomes an idol with a letterhead.
reflect: Is your denomination a means to serve the whole church or an end you serve for its own sake?
What good has your tradition guarded that the wider church needed?
Could you imagine your denomination ceasing to exist if the one church were better served without it?

chapters.title: Cooperation Without Compromise
chapters.summary: The hardest practical question in the theology of unity is how to work together across real differences without either pretending the differences away or letting them justify isolation. There is a narrow road between.
chapters.body:
There are two ways to fail at this, and most of us are tempted toward one of them by temperament. Some of us are wired for warmth and will sacrifice truth to keep the peace; we will partner with anyone, blur every line, call every disagreement a misunderstanding, until our unity means nothing because it stands for nothing. Others are wired for conviction and will sacrifice fellowship to keep the truth pure; we will partner with almost no one, suspect every difference, retreat into a remnant so small and so guarded that we have obeyed half the New Testament while disobeying the other half. The first betrays the truth. The second betrays the body. And we each find our own failure so natural that we mistake it for faithfulness.

The narrow road runs between them, and it is narrow because it requires holding two commitments that are always pulling against each other: a refusal to compromise what is true, and a refusal to withhold fellowship that is owed. Most of us drop one to hold the other. The task is to carry both.

Unity that costs the truth is not unity. Truth that costs all fellowship is not faithfulness. The narrow road runs between them.

Start with the principle that makes cooperation possible at all: the tiering of the last chapters. If all doctrines were first-order, no cooperation across difference would ever be possible, because every disagreement would be a gospel disagreement. But all doctrines are not first-order. The Baptist and the Presbyterian disagree about baptism — a real, second-order difference that keeps them in different congregations — and they agree about the gospel, the deity of Christ, the resurrection, justification, the authority of Scripture, every truth of first importance. On the basis of that vast shared foundation they can do an enormous amount of work together without either compromising a single conviction. They can feed the hungry of their city as one. They can defend the unborn as one. They can stand together for the persecuted, plant churches in unreached places, train pastors, confront a watching world with a united witness to the things that are genuinely one. None of it requires the Baptist to sprinkle an infant or the Presbyterian to wait for a profession of faith. The cooperation costs them nothing they actually believe.

This is the thing the isolationist temperament cannot see. It treats every cooperation as an endorsement, every shared platform as a surrender, as though working alongside a brother on a matter you agree about somehow ratifies the matter you disagree about. It does not. When Paul lists the things of first importance in First Corinthians 15, he is naming the ground on which all true Christians stand together, and standing together on that ground does not erase the second-order differences; it relativizes them. It puts them in their place. To refuse all cooperation until full agreement is reached is to make the second-order an idol, to treat the things we differ on as more decisive than the things we share, which is exactly backward.

But the warm temperament has its own blindness, and I must name it just as plainly. There genuinely is a line. Paul, who pleaded for unity in nearly every letter, drew it without hesitation when the gospel itself was at stake. "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8). He withstood Peter to his face when Peter's conduct denied the gospel of grace (Galatians 2:11). The same apostle who wept over division refused fellowship that would have compromised the truth, because a fellowship that requires you to deny Christ is not fellowship with the body of Christ at all. It is collaboration in a lie.

So the line is real, and the chapter's hardest question is where it falls. The line is not "they disagree with me." The line is not "they make me uncomfortable." The line is not "my tribe would not approve." The line is the gospel itself. Where a partnership would require me to affirm a false gospel, to call evil good, to deny the Christ I confess — there I cannot go, and no appeal to unity can move me, because unity purchased by denying Christ is a counterfeit. But short of that line, the burden of proof falls on the refusal, not the cooperation. I should need a reason not to work with a brother, not a reason to.

That reverses how most of us operate. We treat cooperation as the thing requiring justification and isolation as the safe default. The New Testament treats it the other way. The body is one; that is the default. Fellowship is owed unless the gospel forbids it. The man who withholds it owes an account, not the man who extends it.

I have failed at this from both directions, and the second failure is the one I am most ashamed of. I have refused good cooperation not because the gospel required it but because I was afraid of how it would look to my own people — afraid that partnering with a certain kind of church would cost me standing among the believers whose approval I wanted, afraid of the raised eyebrows in my own tribe. That is not faithfulness to the truth. That is cowardice managing its reputation. I dressed it up as discernment, but it was fear, and the difference between holy refusal and tribal fear is one every leader has to learn to feel in his own gut, because they wear the same clothes.

This is much of what the Pastors Connection Network was built to make possible: cooperation on the vast shared ground without anyone surrendering the convictions that put them in different congregations. A Reformed Baptist and a charismatic and a confessional Presbyterian can labor together for the gospel in a region, can hold one another up, can present a united front to a skeptical world, while still disagreeing — openly, honestly, without pretense — about the things they disagree on. The honesty is the point. We do not pretend the differences away; that would be the warm temperament's failure. We do not let the differences forbid the partnership; that would be the cold temperament's failure. We name them, and we work together anyway, on everything the gospel lets us share.

The narrow road is narrow, and you will fall off it, in one direction or the other, more often than you stay on. I do. But the falling is instructive if you are honest about which way you fell. When you find you have compromised something true to keep a partnership, you fell toward the mush. When you find you have refused a partnership that cost you nothing but the approval of your tribe, you fell toward the pride. Get up. Find the road again. It is the only road that gives the watching world both things at once — a church that believes something, and a church that loves across its differences.

Both. Always both. Anything less is a counterfeit wearing the name of faithfulness.
chapters.verdict: Unity that costs the truth is not unity, and truth that costs all fellowship is not faithfulness; the narrow road runs between them.
reflect: Where could you cooperate with another church tomorrow without compromising anything you believe?
What is the actual line past which you cannot partner, and is it the gospel or merely your comfort?
Have you ever refused good cooperation out of fear of how it would look to your own tribe?

chapters.title: When Division Is Faithful
chapters.summary: There are divisions Scripture commands, and a theology of unity that cannot name them is not a theology of unity at all but a theology of cowardice. The chapter draws the hard line honestly.
chapters.body:
A book that has spent nine chapters pleading for unity must now do the hardest thing of all, or it will have lied to you. It must admit that some divisions are right. That there is a unity which is not faithfulness but compromise, a peace which is not the peace of Christ but the peace of the grave, a togetherness purchased by abandoning the very gospel that makes the church the church. A theology of unity that cannot say this is not a theology of unity. It is a theology of cowardice with the word "love" written over the top.

I have spent this whole book attacking the cold, sectarian temperament that divides too easily. Now I must turn and attack the warm temperament that will not divide at all, because both are failures, and the second hides more easily behind the language of grace.

The unity Christ prayed for is unity in the truth. He prayed, in the same chapter, "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth" (John 17:17). The oneness of verse twenty-one is not a oneness in spite of the truth or alongside it but in it. There is no other kind in the mind of Jesus. A unity that requires the church to stop believing the gospel is not the unity He asked the Father for. It is its counterfeit, and the counterfeit has done as much damage as the division.

A peace that requires abandoning Christ is not the peace He left us.

So when does division become faithful? Scripture is not vague about this, however much we wish it were. Paul names it plainly. When another gospel is preached — a message that is not the saving message of Christ crucified and risen — the response is not patient fellowship but a curse: "let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:9). When a man stirs up division by teaching contrary to the apostolic doctrine, the instruction is to warn him twice and then have nothing more to do with him (Titus 3:10). When false teachers deny the Lord who bought them, John writes that we are not even to greet them, lest we share in their wicked work (2 John 10–11). These are not the words of a church indifferent to unity. They are the words of the same New Testament that pleads for it, drawing the line where the line must be drawn.

The line is the gospel. Always the gospel. Not the second-order differences we have spent this book learning to live alongside — not baptism, not church government, not eschatology, not worship style. Those are differences within the one faith, and to divide the body over them is the sectarian sin. The line falls at the gospel itself: the deity and humanity of Christ, His atoning death and bodily resurrection, salvation by grace through faith, the authority of God's word. Where these are denied, the issue is no longer fellowship within the church but whether the church is even present. You cannot divide from someone who has already departed. You can only acknowledge what has happened and refuse to pretend otherwise.

History gives us the pattern. When Athanasius stood against the Arians in the fourth century — *Athanasius contra mundum*, Athanasius against the world — he was not being a divisive man. He was refusing a false peace. The Arians were willing to be united; they only asked the church to leave the full deity of Christ an open question, to soften the language, to make room. Athanasius would not, and he was exiled five times for the refusal, and the church remembers him as a hero precisely because he understood that some unity is bought at too high a price. Had he taken the peace on offer, the church would have been united around a Christ who was not God, which is to say united around nothing worth being united around.

This is the discernment the chapter demands, and it is the inverse of the discernment of chapter six. There the danger was elevating a secondary matter to primary status and dividing over a fence. Here the danger is the opposite: demoting a primary matter to secondary status and refusing to divide when the gospel itself is at stake. The cold heart fences off too much. The warm heart fences off too little. Both have lost the gospel — one by guarding things that are not it, the other by surrendering the thing that is.

Bonhoeffer is the witness here, because he lived it at the highest cost. When much of the German church bent itself to the Nazi state, draping the cross with the swastika and excluding believers of Jewish descent, the question was not one of secondary preference. It was whether the church would remain the church of Jesus Christ or become an organ of an idolatrous state. The Confessing Church divided from the official church not out of pride but out of necessity, because a unity that required denying Christ's lordship over all peoples was no unity worth keeping. Bonhoeffer chose the division and finally chose the death, and history has vindicated him against the churchmen who chose the peace. There are times when the man who divides is the faithful one and the man who keeps the peace is the apostate.

But — and I will not let go of this — the warning runs in both directions, and I must turn it on myself before I turn it on you. The same passages that authorize faithful division have authorized ten thousand unfaithful ones. Every petty schismatic in church history has quoted Galatians 1. Every man who divided a congregation over his wounded pride has told himself he was contending for the faith. The flesh is endlessly inventive at dressing its preferences as principles and its quarrels as faithfulness. And so the reflection question is the one that matters most: can you tell the difference, in yourself, between a division the gospel requires and a division your pride desires? Because they feel identical from the inside. Both feel like conviction. Both feel like courage. Only one is.

I have divided "for the truth" when the truth was really just my preference. I have walked away from fellowship and called it faithfulness when it was wounded ego. I have quoted the verses about false teachers to justify a coldness that the gospel never authorized. The capacity for self-deception here is bottomless, and the only guard I know is a relentless self-suspicion, a willingness to ask whether the gospel is actually at stake or whether I have merely been crossed, whether Christ is being denied or whether I am merely being inconvenienced.

So here is where the book has been heading, and it does not resolve, because the truth does not let it. The same church that must learn to stay together across its differences must also know when to divide for the gospel, and the line between is fine enough that only the humble can find it and only the prayerful can hold it. We will get it wrong in both directions. We will divide when we should have stayed and stay when we should have divided. The remedy is not a formula. It is a life lived close enough to Christ that we can tell His voice from our own resentment.

The unity He prayed for is unity in the truth. Guard the truth, and you may have to divide. Guard your pride, and you will divide and call it truth. Learn the difference, or you will spend your life serving the wrong master while quoting the right verses.
chapters.verdict: The unity Christ prayed for is unity in the truth; a peace that requires abandoning Him is not the peace He left us.
reflect: Can you tell the difference in yourself between a division required by the gospel and a division driven by pride?
Where might your love of peace be tempting you to tolerate what the gospel forbids?
Have you ever divided "for the truth" when the truth was really just your preference?

chapters.title: That They May Be One
chapters.summary: The book returns to the prayer it began with, no longer as accusation but as commission. Unity is not a program we complete but a prayer we are answered into, and the answering begins in us.
chapters.body:
We end where we began, in the garden's shadow, on the last night, with the prayer still hanging in the air. "That they may all be one" (John 17:21). I called it, in the first chapter, the prayer we have spent twenty centuries not answering. I want to end by saying something harder and more hopeful than accusation. The prayer is not only a verdict on the church. It is a commission to it. And the commission has our names on it.

Because here is what I have come to believe after all these pages. The unity Jesus prayed for is not finally a program the church completes. It is a prayer the church is answered into. He asked the Father for it, and the Father does not refuse the Son, and so the oneness of the church is, at the deepest level, a thing being accomplished by God in answer to the prayer of God — the Spirit drawing the scattered body toward the unity it already possesses in Christ. We are not the authors of that unity. We are not strong enough or good enough to manufacture it, and every human attempt to engineer the reunion of the church has either failed or produced a uniformity that was worse than the division it cured.

But we are not nothing in it either. Prayers like this one are answered through people, in people, by people who let themselves become the instruments of the answer. And so the question the prayer finally puts to each of us is not "how will the church achieve unity," which is too big for any of us and belongs to God. The question is smaller and sharper and unavoidable: in the answering of this prayer, will I be an instrument or an obstacle? Will the Spirit's work toward oneness move through me or have to work around me?

He prayed that they may be one. The question He left us is whether we will be the answer or the obstacle.

I cannot reunite the church. Neither can you. But I can refuse to widen the cracks. I can stop telling the story that makes the other church look foolish. I can reconcile the relationship with the brother across the line that I have let stay broken because mending it would cost my pride. I can grant honor to the part of the body my tribe finds embarrassing. I can hold my real convictions as convictions without making them the boundary of the kingdom. I can confess, in the small daily ways the watching world reads more closely than any creed, that the body of Christ is one. None of that reunites Christendom. All of it is the prayer being answered, one stubborn act of love at a time, in the only place any of us actually has authority — our own conduct toward the brothers and sisters God has actually put in front of us.

Newbigin said the congregation is the hermeneutic of the gospel, the lens through which the world reads the message. I would add that the relationships between congregations are the hermeneutic of the gospel's power, the proof that the message does what it claims. A single church living the gospel well is a sermon. A town full of churches that love one another across their differences is an argument the skeptic cannot easily answer, and I know, because I was that skeptic, and it was finally that argument that I could not answer. Not the cleverness of any apologist. The stubborn, visible, costly love of Christians who treated their differences as a family treats its quarrels — real, but never grounds for ceasing to be family.

I think of the reflection question I cannot escape myself: if my church vanished tomorrow, would the one body of Christ in my town be visibly poorer, and would the other churches even notice? It is a brutal question, because it exposes whether I have been building my congregation as a member of the body or as a rival to it. A church that competes with the others would not be missed by them; its disappearance would be their gain. A church that genuinely serves the one body would leave a wound in the whole if it vanished, and the other pastors would grieve, because they had come to depend on it as one depends on a part of one's own flesh. I want to build that kind of church. I have not always built that kind of church. The PCN exists, in part, because I grew tired of building the rival kind and wanted to spend the rest of my ministry building the other.

Let me leave you with the weight rather than the relief, because the prayer does not relieve and I will not pretend it does.

The church Jesus prayed for is one. The church the watching world sees is in pieces, and each piece is largely satisfied that it holds the center while the others drift at the edges. Between those two churches — the one He prayed for and the one we have made — runs the whole distance of our disobedience and the whole reach of His patience. He has not withdrawn the prayer. It still stands, spoken once and never canceled, hanging over every divided congregation and every competing denomination and every pastor who finds it easier to dismiss a brother than to love him. That they may be one. He is still praying it, the Scripture says, interceding at the right hand of the Father, and the Spirit is still answering it, drawing the body slowly, against all our resistance, toward the oneness it already has in Him.

The only question is the one with your name on it. When the Spirit moves to answer the prayer of the Son in your town, in your church, in the relationship you have let stay broken, in the rival you have refused to call brother — when that movement reaches you, will it find an instrument or an obstacle? Will the answer move through you, or will it have to go around?

I do not know your answer. I am still working out my own, and I will be working it out until I die, and I will get it wrong more than I get it right. But I know this. He prayed it on His last night, when a man says only the things that were always load-bearing. He prayed that we would be one. And He is waiting, with a patience longer than our division, to see what we will do with the prayer He prayed last.

That they may be one. Carry it out of here. Do not set it down.
chapters.verdict: He prayed that they may be one; the question He left us is whether we will be the answer or the obstacle.
reflect: After ten chapters, what is the one division in your own life you can no longer justify?
Who is the brother or sister, across some line, you have been treating as less than family?
If your church vanished tomorrow, would the one body of Christ in your town be visibly poorer — and would the other churches even notice?
